qs.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS) occurring in patients with cirrhosis?
o: Urine sodium less than 10 mmol/L
Marked intravascular volume depletion
Intrinsic structural renal disease on biopsy
Elevated urine sodium greater than 40 mmol/L
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is characterized by a low urine sodium of less than 10 mmol/L, normal intravascular volume, and the absence of intrinsic renal disease. A high urine sodium would point toward acute tubular necrosis rather than HRS.

qs.q: What is recognized as the only definitive cure for Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
o: Serial large-volume therapeutic paracentesis
High-dose intravenous furosemide therapy
Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure
Definitive orthotopic liver transplantation
qs.e: Liver transplantation is noted as the only definitive cure for hepatorenal syndrome, although vasoactive agents and TIPS can be used as bridging or supportive measures. Diuretics are typically withdrawn.

qs.q: A patient with refractory ascites and portal hypertension develops renal impairment. Which specific laboratory finding characterizes Hepatorenal Syndrome?
o: Elevated intravascular volume status
Creatinine clearance above 80 ml/min
Presence of intrinsic renal disease
Urine sodium less than 10 mmol/L
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is characterized by a urine sodium of less than 10 mmol/L along with normal intravascular volume and no intrinsic renal disease. An elevated creatinine clearance is incorrect since renal impairment features reduced clearance.

qs.q: Which finding is typically observed in the urine of a patient suffering from hepatorenal syndrome?
o: Alkaline with prominent glucosuria and high bilirubinuria
Hypoosmolar with massive proteinuria and high sodium levels
Isosthenuric with active hematuria and cellular casts present
Hyperosmolar and protein-negative with very low sodium
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome presents with functional renal failure where urine is characteristically hyperosmolar, protein-negative, and low in sodium due to intense renal vasoconstriction. Intrinsic kidney damage or acute tubular necrosis are excluded.

qs.q: A patient with advanced liver disease presents with oliguria, azotemia, and a low urine sodium level, consistent with hepatorenal syndrome. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the renal failure?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of the renal parenchyma
Obstructive uropathy secondary to retroperitoneal fibrosis
Primary glomerular deposition of circulating immune complexes
Marked peripheral vasodilatation leading to renal hypoperfusion
qs.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is driven by marked peripheral vasodilatation and effective hypovolemia, causing reflex renal vasoconstriction. It is a functional renal failure occurring in the presence of normal kidney structure.

faq.a: Renal vasoconstriction reduces filtration and the kidney conserves sodium, giving a low urine sodium.

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with cirrhosis develops oliguria and creatinine rises to 2.6 mg/dL in 3 days. What is the next step? — Identify precipitating infection, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and give albumin.
In a patient with cirrhosis and rising creatinine, how do you distinguish HRS from ATN? — Check urine sodium (<10 mmol/L) and FeNa (<1 %); ATN shows higher values and casts.
A patient with HRS is started on terlipressin. Why is this drug avoided in patients with heart failure? — Terlipressin causes systemic vasoconstriction, worsening cardiac output.
What laboratory finding would rule out HRS? — Presence of granular casts on urinalysis indicates intrinsic renal injury.
Why is diuretic therapy stopped in HRS? — Diuretics worsen intravascular volume depletion and precipitate HRS.
Which of the following is a contraindication to terlipressin? — Severe ischemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension.
How does spontaneous bacterial peritonitis precipitate HRS? — Infection triggers systemic inflammation and vasodilation, reducing effective arterial volume.

ai.summary: A functional renal failure that develops in advanced liver disease, characterised by severe vasoconstriction of renal circulation and low urinary sodium. It is diagnosed by exclusion of intrinsic kidney disease and treated with vasoconstrictors and supportive care.

b: Serum creatinine rise >0.3 mg/dL in 48 h or >50 % in 1 week (type 1)
No intrarenal pathology on urinalysis (no casts)
sections.p: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a rapidly progressive renal failure that occurs in patients with advanced cirrhosis or acute liver failure, in the absence of intrinsic kidney disease. Diagnosis requires a rising serum creatinine, low urinary sodium (<10 mmol/L), FeNa <1 % and no evidence of shock, nephrotoxic drugs or obstruction.

t.b: Measures kidney filtration; a rise >0.3 mg/dL in 48 h indicates acute kidney injury
Low value (<10 mmol/L) shows prerenal state
Fractional excretion of sodium <1 % confirms prerenal cause
Absence of granular or muddy brown casts rules out ATN

b: Type 1: doubling of creatinine in <2 weeks or >2.5 mg/dL
Type 2: creatinine 1.5–2.5 mg/dL, stable over weeks
sections.p: The International Ascites Club classifies HRS into type 1 (rapid, creatinine >2.5 mg/dL or doubling in <2 weeks) and type 2 (slow, creatinine 1.5–2.5 mg/dL with refractory ascites).

The primary driver is severe splanchnic vasodilation leading to systemic arterial underfilling and renal vasoconstriction. Common precipitating factors in low‑resource settings include bacterial infections (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), gastrointestinal bleeding, dehydration, and nephrotoxic drugs.

Patients have advanced liver disease features (ascites, spider naevi, encephalopathy) plus sudden oliguria, rising creatinine, and low urine sodium. Blood pressure may be normal or low, and peripheral oedema is often prominent.
Investigations aim to confirm HRS and exclude other causes. In low‑resource settings, focus on basic labs and bedside tests.
HRS is a medical emergency; complications include metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, hepatic encephalopathy, and death if untreated. Watch for sudden worsening of creatinine, hypotension, or bleeding.

Treat the precipitating cause first, then give vasoconstrictor therapy (terlipressin or norepinephrine) plus albumin to restore effective circulating volume. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and monitor renal function closely.
Monitor serum creatinine and urine output daily. Prevent recurrence by treating infections promptly, avoiding nephrotoxins, and considering early liver transplantation.

b: ATN – high urine sodium, muddy brown casts
sections.p: Acute tubular necrosis, pre‑renal azotemia from dehydration, and hepatorenal syndrome type 2. Distinguish by urine sodium, FeNa, and response to vasoconstrictors.
In cirrhosis, serum creatinine may underestimate true GFR; low urine sodium can be seen in diuretic use; albumin levels may be low due to malnutrition.
